title: Product design for founders who are also the first user
metaTitle: Product design for startups, founder first
excerpt: Product design for startups starts from a split: the founder's own use is evidence, and the next user's job is the spec. Habit is not the whole product.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The goals on the page are the next person's job, separate from the founder's habits.
caption: Write the job before you defend the screen. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a founder design the product around their own workflow?
faqs.answer: Use your workflow as evidence of the job, then test which steps a new person still needs. Keep the steps that complete the job. Set aside shortcuts that exist only because you remember an earlier version. Your fluency is not a feature you can ship.

faqs.question: How many people do I need to watch before I change the design?
faqs.answer: One session with someone who has the job and does not know your interface will expose the assumptions you can no longer see. It will not represent every customer. Run a second session when the first person was too close to you, such as a cofounder.

faqs.question: When should I overrule that feedback?
faqs.answer: Overrule a request when it would break the job for the next person, and write the reason in a sentence. A confirmation on an action that cannot be undone is a product decision. Keeping a control because you like the old order is a habit, and it has to earn its place.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Product design for startups, when the founder is also the first user, starts from a split. Your own use is evidence. The next person's job is the spec. You know the shortcuts, the jargon, and the reason a strange control exists. The next person arrives with a task and almost none of that history.

That split is the work. Keep the parts of your behavior that reveal the real job. Set aside the parts that exist because you built the thing and can tolerate it. A product that feels obvious to its author and opaque to the first customer is usually a diary of the author's habits, published by accident.

## Write the job before you defend a screen

Before you open the design file, write the next user's job in a sentence that does not mention your interface. A coach checks who has not paid before the session. A recruiter sees which conversations stalled. If the sentence only makes sense when your screen is in front of you, you have described the product, not the job.

Put your last real session next to that sentence. List what you clicked, in order, including the steps you skipped because you already knew the answer. The skipped steps are the interesting ones. They are either unnecessary for everyone, or they are necessary and you are doing them from memory. Memory is not a control you can hand to someone else.

Do this on paper if the file tempts you to rearrange buttons instead of finishing the sentence. The sentence is the constraint. Screens come after it, and they have to serve it. A founder who starts in the component library will design a familiar product and call the familiarity research.

## Separate habit from the job

Mark each step you took as one of three things.

1. The step is the job. Removing it would mean the person cannot finish.
2. The step is your habit. You do it because the first version taught you to, and a new person would not miss it.
3. The step is a repair. You do it to undo something the product got wrong, such as clearing a filter you did not mean to set.

Keep the first list short. Question the second list in the next design. Treat the third list as defects, even if you have stopped noticing them. A founder who has used a rough build for months develops a private operating manual. New users do not receive a copy of that manual, and they should not need one.

Nielsen Norman Group's 2011 research on web pages is a warning about patience. It measured page visits, not your product, and the pattern is still the one to design for. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when the value is unclear, and they have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they do visit. [The article](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) argues that value has to be clear quickly if you want someone to stay. A founder will sit for an hour inside a confusing tool because the tool is theirs. The next user will not owe you that hour.

## Watch one person who is not you

Sit with someone who has the job and does not have your habits. Give them the job sentence. Do not explain the interface first. Watch where they hesitate, and write down the moment they ask what a label means. Those questions are the spec you did not know you were missing.

Wait before you rescue them. Rescue in the first minute teaches you nothing about the screen. After they finish or stall, ask what they thought the screen was for. If their answer differs from your sentence, the gap is the design problem. Their preferred color is not.

One session will not stand in for every customer. It will catch the assumptions that have become invisible to you, which is the reason to do it before you add another screen. Run a second session when the first person was unusually close to your world. A stranger to the product is the better witness. A cofounder is a second founder.

## What you may keep from your own use

Keep a flow that matches the job sentence and that the other person could finish. Keep vocabulary the customer already uses. If your buyers say "pipeline," that word is theirs. If an earlier prototype said "pipeline" and your buyers say "deals," change the word. Your fluency with the old term is not a branding decision.

Keep density when the job is dense. A scheduling grid or a list of applicants can hold a lot if the person came to scan it. Density is not the same as showing every control you personally use. Extra controls can live one step away, named for what they do, so the main view stays the job.

Write the decisions beside the flow. Which step is required. Which label changed because of the session. Which idea you are postponing because it served a habit. That page is a spec someone else can build without interviewing you from the beginning again. It is also a spec you can argue with later, because the reasons are still on the page.

## When your experience should overrule the session

Sometimes the witness misunderstands the domain, and you know it because you have done the job. Overrule them when their request would break the job for the next person. Say the reason in one sentence. "We are keeping the confirmation because a mistaken send cannot be undone." That is a product decision. "I like the old order of these fields" is a habit, and it has to earn a place beside the job.

You remain a source of defects and of priorities, because you use the product on days when nobody is watching a session. The discipline is to label what you bring. Evidence goes in the notes as evidence. A request to preserve your shortcut goes in as a shortcut. Labels keep the spec from slowly becoming your autobiography.

A first version can respect this split and still feel complete, if the path you keep is finished rather than merely short. That is the next decision. Read [how to design an MVP that feels finished](/blog/mvp-that-feels-finished). A narrow path with a blank start, a clear failure, and a real success will teach you more than a wide product only you can operate.
